headline: Keurig smart coffee maker uploaded 1TB of data in 10 days, baffling IT pro
summary: An IT professional discovered his parents' Keurig K-Supreme SMART coffee maker uploaded over 1TB of data in just 10 days, causing network slowdowns. While initially suspected to be a bug or DRM, the issue was temporarily resolved by rebooting and isolating the
details: An IT professional reported that his parents' Keurig K-Supreme SMART coffee maker uploaded a staggering 1TB of data over their Wi-Fi in just 10 days. This massive data transfer saturated their access point and significantly slowed down their home network.

The user, known as @NomadsGalaxy on X, shared a UniFi screenshot showing 1,008.45GB of upstream traffic from the Keurig device over a period of 10 days and 9 hours. This averages out to about 9 Mbps upstream, a data rate comparable to 27 times the amount reported in a similar LG washer incident from 2024.

The K-Supreme SMART model features BrewID, which uses Wi-Fi for app control, voice commands via Alexa and Google Home, and recognizing Keurig-made pods. The IT pro initially speculated that the excessive data might be related to "DRM waiting to be enabled."

Later in the X thread, Nomad acknowledged that the UniFi system might have misreported the actual upload, suggesting it was mostly local junk data. Rebooting the coffee maker and placing it in a segregated VLAN on the network temporarily resolved the issue.

Keurig's open-source notice indicates their IoT devices use Microsoft Azure RTOS. Typically, data sent to the cloud includes small packets of information like power state, brew state, pod recognition results, and software version, making a 1TB upload highly indicative of a malfunction.

Smart brewers are designed to keep 14 days of brew history and sync it when connected, with Keurig-made pods earning points for users. Reports from 2022 also indicated Keurig shared brewing data with K-Cup brands for personalized marketing efforts.

This incident highlights ongoing concerns regarding clandestine data gathering by IoT devices, a topic that has recently seen other manufacturers like LG face scrutiny over their smart appliances and TVs.

headline: Run a Gemini alternative completely offline on your Android phone with PocketPal AI
summary: PocketPal AI allows users to download and run large language models like Gemma directly on their device, offering privacy and offline functionality at the cost of speed and real-time data access.
details: PocketPal AI is an open-source Android application that enables users to run large language models (LLMs) like Gemma, Qwen, and Phi directly on their phones, without requiring an internet connection. This offers a significant privacy advantage, as conversations and data remain entirely on the device.

The app supports GGUF models from Hugging Face and utilizes llama.cpp to leverage the phone's CPU, GPU, or NPU hardware for inference. Users need at least 6GB of RAM for smaller models and 8GB or more for larger ones, with models consuming significant storage space.

To get started, users download a model within the app, then load it into memory to begin chatting. The process is straightforward, with PocketPal AI available on the Google Play Store, though more technical options like MLC Chat or Google AI Edge Gallery also exist.

While the offline functionality and enhanced privacy are key benefits, there are trade-offs. Responses from local LLMs are noticeably slower than cloud-based alternatives, and smaller on-device models may not match the capabilities of the largest cloud models.

Additionally, being completely offline means the AI cannot access current information, news, or breaking stories. It's a powerful tool for private, on-device conversations but doesn't replace cloud-connected AIs for tasks requiring up-to-date external data.

PocketPal AI also offers features like 'Pals' (preconfigured AI personalities) and voice options, allowing for a more customized and interactive experience. The ability to switch between different downloaded models provides users with greater control over their AI assistant.
